writeup.headline: Maravai rates Sell: a powerful share-price rally sits on top of losses, cash burn and a full valuation.
writeup.thesis: Maravai scores 36, a Sell, because weak fundamentals outweigh very strong price momentum. Growth scores 26: latest-quarter revenue growth of 8.5% year on year still leaves a TTM revenue decline of 5.0%, and growth slowed by 32.0 pp from the previous quarter. Quality (20) and balance sheet (19) are weak, with a gross margin of 34.9%, an operating margin of -56.1%, an FCF margin of -18.6%, stock-based compensation at 14.3% of revenue, and cash covering only 0.48 times debt while free cash flow is negative. Valuation scores 9: P/S of 6.0 is high in absolute terms for a loss-making business, FCF yield is 8.1 pp below the 10-year Treasury yield, and the stock is expensive against its own history, more expensive than at 49 of the last 56 month-ends on P/S (P/FCF and EV/EBIT not comparable). Offsetting this, trend scores 97, with shares up 129.0% from 12 months ago to 1 month ago and price 5.6% below its 52-week high, and news is mildly positive (59) on a new Buy initiation and a second China CleanCap patent.
key_risks: Continued operating losses and negative free cash flow could pressure a balance sheet where cash is 0.48 times debt.
The sharp rally (price 63.7% above its 200-day average) could reverse if Q3 results on Nov 4 disappoint.
Ongoing dilution, with diluted share count up 2.6% year on year and SBC at 14.3% of revenue.
Customer concentration, with Pfizer at 12.2% of revenue in the first half of 2026, plus the pending 2025 securities class action.
what_would_change: A rise of 9 points to 45 would lift the rating to Hold, most plausibly through sustained revenue growth and improving margins and cash flow in the growth and quality factors.
A drop of 7 points below 30 would mean Strong Sell, for example if the trend score falls from 97 as momentum fades.
Q3 results on Nov 4 meeting or beating the reiterated $205–215M revenue and raised $33–35M adjusted EBITDA guidance would support the score; a cut would weigh on it.
A lower share price relative to sales would improve the very low valuation score.
